evidence.claim: From the Desert to the Tall Pines is a scenic byway through central Arizona’s changing plant communities.
evidence.quote: Visitors will be introduced to the complex ecosystems that contribute to their quality of life as they pass through various biotic communities along the 74 miles of SR-288 designated as a Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service identifies that variety of landscapes as the route’s theme.
evidence.quote: From the Desert to the Tall Pines Scenic Byway provides forest visitors the opportunity to experience the variety of landscapes and resources that central Arizona provides. The theme From the Desert to the Tall Pines reflects this emphasis.

evidence.claim: SR 288 crosses mountainous terrain, and most of the highway is unpaved.
evidence.quote: Currently, most of SR 288 is unpaved.

evidence.claim: Young has paved stretches within and north of town, but no fully paved connection to another highway.
evidence.quote: SR 288 is paved within and north of the town, totaling about 10 miles (16 km) of pavement, but there is no fully paved road connecting Young with other highways.

evidence.claim: SR 288 became a state route in 1959 and received scenic-road designation in 2001.
evidence.quote: The route was established in 1959 as a state route. The highway received scenic road designation in 2001.

evidence.claim: The numbered highway ends at Chamberlain Trail in Young; the roadway continues north as a National Forest road.
evidence.quote: The northern terminus is located at an intersection with Chamberlain Trail in Young.  The roadway continues on as a National Forest road.

evidence.claim: The wider landscape includes the Sierra Ancha, a range between Pleasant Valley and Roosevelt Lake with deep canyons and few improved roads.
evidence.quote: It lies between Roosevelt Lake to the south, the Tonto Basin to the west, Cherry Creek to the east, and Pleasant Valley to the north.

evidence.claim: Traveling north to south, Willow Springs Lake beside SR 260 provides a Rim-side excursion before the forest-road approach to Young.
evidence.quote: immediately adjacent to SR 260.

evidence.claim: FR 512 leads south from SR 260 to Young in Pleasant Valley.
evidence.quote: From Arizona State Route 260 between mile markers 284 and 285 (east of Christopher Creek and west of Heber/Overgaard), go south along FR512 for about 26 miles (42 km).

evidence.claim: Beyond town, SR 288 passes Rock House and reaches SR 188 southeast of Roosevelt Lake.
evidence.quote: The southern terminus of SR 288 is located on SR 188 southeast of Theodore Roosevelt Lake.  The highway heads north from this intersection through mountainous terrain as it heads towards Young. It passes through the community of Rock House.

evidence.claim: SR 288 crosses mountainous terrain
evidence.quote: The highway heads north from this intersection through mountainous terrain

evidence.claim: with deep canyons and few improved roads.
evidence.quote: The Sierra Ancha is penetrated by few improved roads, and the range is cut by numerous deep, spectacular canyons

evidence.claim: Young in Pleasant Valley.
evidence.quote: The community is set in the Pleasant Valley

evidence.claim: Not all sections are paved, and several areas receive heavy winter snowfall. Check ADOT for road closures.
evidence.quote: Check ADOT's website for road closures. Not all sections are paved. During winter months, several areas receive heavy snowfall.

evidence.claim: Willow Springs Lake has no permanent inflow: annual snowmelt supplies its water.
evidence.quote: Willow Springs Lake has no permanent inflow, but receives enough snow melt every year to keep the lake full.

evidence.claim: The Arizona Game and Fish Department created the lake in 1967 for public water recreation.
evidence.quote: In 1967, the Arizona Game and Fish Department created Willow Springs Lake in order to provide water based recreational opportunities for the public.

evidence.claim: Its 158 acres occupy a canyon on top of the Mogollon Rim beside SR 260.
evidence.quote: It is a canyon-bound lake located on the Mogollon Rim

evidence.claim: The department holds the lake’s sole water rights, and most of the year there is no spill downstream.
evidence.quote: The Arizona Game and Fish Department holds sole water rights to the lake. Unless spill-off occurs during the spring, no water is released downstream for irrigation or other uses. Most of the year, no spill occurs.

evidence.claim: When water does spill, it follows Willow Springs Canyon to Woods Canyon, where the two drainages form Chevelon Creek.
evidence.quote: When spill occurs, it drains down Willow Springs Canyon for 3.4 miles and merges with Woods Canyon to form Chevelon Creek.

evidence.claim: Its 158 acres
evidence.quote: a surface area of 158 acres

evidence.claim: beside SR 260.
evidence.quote: immediately adjacent to SR 260.

evidence.claim: Vehicle access is seasonal: the lake is accessible by paved Forest Road 149 from April through November and inaccessible to vehicles from December through March.
evidence.quote: Willow Springs Lake is accessible via paved Forest Road 149 from April through November. From December through March, the lake freezes over and is inaccessible for vehicles.

evidence.claim: Young sits in Pleasant Valley, drained by Cherry Creek toward the Salt River.
evidence.quote: The community is set in the Pleasant Valley, drained to the southeast by Cherry Creek, a tributary of the Salt River.

evidence.claim: It was a center of the Pleasant Valley War, the conflict involving the Graham and Tewksbury families.
evidence.quote: Young played a central part in the Pleasant Valley War

evidence.claim: The two families initially opposed cattleman James Stinson together; the conflict later drew in other cattlemen, sheepmen, hired gunmen and law officers.
evidence.quote: Although the feud was originally fought between the Tewksburys and the Grahams against the well-established cattleman James Stinson, it soon involved other cattlemen associations, sheepmen, hired guns, cowboys and Arizona lawmen.

evidence.claim: Many of the men murdered in the conflict are buried in Young’s cemetery.
evidence.quote: The graves of many of the murdered men can still be seen in the Young, Arizona, cemetery

evidence.claim: The Forest Service identifies Pleasant Valley Cemetery as a common stop along the byway.
evidence.quote: Common destination stops include Pleasant Valley Cemetery and various scenic overlooks.

evidence.claim: the conflict involving the Graham and Tewksbury families.
evidence.quote: The conflict involved two feuding families, the Grahams and the Tewksburys.

evidence.claim: Both families raised cattle; the Tewksburys later added sheep to their operations.
evidence.quote: The Grahams were ranchers, while the Tewksburys, who were part Native American, started their operations as cattle ranchers before branching out to sheep.

evidence.claim: Both families raised cattle
evidence.quote: Tom Graham and John D. Tewksbury started out as friends but things changed when a big cattleman named James Stinson came into Pleasant Valley. His large herd quickly started to occupy many areas of grazing land, dominating the ranches built by the two families.

evidence.claim: The range’s Western Apache name, Dził Nteel, means “Wide Flat Mountain”; Sierra Ancha is Spanish for “broad range.”

flags: The Forest Service calls all 74 byway miles SR 288, while the highway page ends SR 288 in Young and the Young page identifies FR 512 northward. Kept highway and corridor distinct; omitted an exact corridor mileage from prose. ADOT cache is only Wayback navigation.

Moments run north to south in increasing strip-mile order. Willow Springs is a separate excursion beside SR 260, not a stop on SR 288. Sierra Ancha coordinates identify the range, not an overlook or trailhead; no direct roadside access is implied.
Young page dates the war 1887–1897; the war page gives 1882–1892. Dates, disputed incidents and a precise death toll are omitted.

No current claim was dropped for lack of cache support. Ice fishing and the four-wheel-drive recommendation were omitted as nonessential activity advice and secondary-source logistics; the Forest Service supports the unpaved-road and winter-snow note.
Willow Springs seasonal vehicle access is supported only by a secondary source; no current site-manager page is available. Checked dates record local cache review, not live confirmation.
